checks.title: Password maximum age is 365 days or less
checks.rationale: Forcing periodic password changes limits the window an already-compromised password stays useful, though CIS notes this is less important when MFA is in use.
checks.evidence: /etc/login.defs PASS_MAX_DAYS 99999 (expected 0 < PASS_MAX_DAYS <= 365)
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_MAX_DAYS 365' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --maxdays 365 <user>)

checks.title: Password minimum age is at least 1 day
checks.rationale: Without a minimum age, a user can immediately change a new password back to their old one, defeating password-history rotation policies.
checks.evidence: /etc/login.defs PASS_MIN_DAYS 0 (expected PASS_MIN_DAYS >= 1)
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_MIN_DAYS 1' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --mindays 1 <user>)

checks.title: Password expiration warning is at least 7 days
checks.rationale: Warning users before their password expires avoids surprise lockouts, which otherwise tend to get 'fixed' by disabling expiry entirely - a worse outcome.
checks.evidence: /etc/login.defs PASS_WARN_AGE 7
checks.remediation: Set 'PASS_WARN_AGE 7' in /etc/login.defs (existing accounts also need: chage --warndays 7 <user>)

checks.title: No accounts have an empty password field in /etc/shadow
checks.rationale: An empty password field (2nd colon-delimited field in /etc/shadow) means PAM may allow that account to log in with no password at all, depending on nullok settings.
checks.evidence: /etc/shadow could not be read (requires root) - cannot verify password fields.
checks.remediation: passwd -l <user>  # lock any account found with an empty password field, or set a real password with passwd <user>

checks.title: No duplicate UID 0 (root-equivalent) accounts exist besides root
checks.rationale: Any account sharing UID 0 has full root privileges regardless of its username - this is a classic backdoor technique and should never occur outside of 'root' itself.
checks.evidence: UID 0 accounts: root
checks.remediation: Investigate any extra UID-0 account immediately; usually: usermod -u <new-unique-uid> <account>  or delete it with userdel if unauthorized.

checks.title: Root account's default group is GID 0
checks.rationale: root's primary group should be the root group (GID 0), matching standard system convention; a different primary group is unusual and worth investigating (could indicate tampering or a broken account migration).
checks.evidence: root:x:0:0
checks.remediation: usermod -g 0 root

checks.title: No duplicate UIDs exist in /etc/passwd
checks.rationale: Two accounts sharing a UID are indistinguishable to the kernel and most tools - files 'owned' by one are equally accessible to both, and audit logs can't tell them apart.
checks.evidence: Checked 27 entries in /etc/passwd. No duplicates found.
checks.remediation: Assign each account a unique UID with usermod -u <new-uid> <name>.

checks.title: No duplicate GIDs exist in /etc/group
checks.rationale: Two groups sharing a GID grant identical file access to both groups' members, which usually indicates a configuration mistake rather than an intentional access grant.
checks.evidence: Checked 59 entries in /etc/group. No duplicates found.
checks.remediation: Assign each group a unique GID with groupmod -g <new-gid> <name>.

checks.title: No duplicate usernames exist in /etc/passwd
checks.rationale: Duplicate usernames create ambiguity about which entry (and which UID) applies for tools that look up by name, which can be abused to run as an unintended UID.
checks.evidence: Checked 27 entries in /etc/passwd. No duplicates found.
checks.remediation: Rename or remove the duplicate entry so each username appears once.

checks.title: No duplicate group names exist in /etc/group
checks.rationale: Same ambiguity risk as duplicate usernames, applied to group name lookups.
checks.evidence: Checked 59 entries in /etc/group. No duplicates found.
checks.remediation: Rename or remove the duplicate entry so each group name appears once.

checks.title: root's PATH does not contain a relative or world-writable directory
checks.rationale: A relative entry (like '.') or a world-writable directory in root's PATH lets any local user plant a malicious binary that root might execute by name, a classic privilege-escalation trick.
checks.evidence: PATH='/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/games:/usr/local/games' (evaluated for the account running this audit, UID 1000)
checks.remediation: Remove any relative or world-writable directory from root's PATH in /root/.bashrc, /root/.profile, or /etc/profile.

checks.title: No interactive user has a .netrc file in their home directory
checks.rationale: A .netrc file can store plaintext credentials for automated FTP/HTTP logins; if present it's a high-value target for any attacker who gains even unprivileged read access to that home directory.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user home director(ies) for .netrc. None found.
checks.remediation: Review and remove any .netrc file found: rm ~<user>/.netrc

checks.title: No interactive user has a .forward file in their home directory
checks.rationale: A .forward file silently forwards a user's mail to another address (potentially external) - a common way to exfiltrate sensitive mail (e.g. password reset emails) after an account is compromised.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user home director(ies) for .forward. None found.
checks.remediation: Review and remove any .forward file found: rm ~<user>/.forward

checks.title: No interactive user has a .rhosts file in their home directory
checks.rationale: A .rhosts file grants passwordless rlogin/rsh trust to listed remote hosts/users - a legacy trust mechanism with no cryptographic authentication that should never be present on a hardened host.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user home director(ies) for .rhosts. None found.
checks.remediation: Review and remove any .rhosts file found: rm ~<user>/.rhosts

checks.title: All interactive users' home directories exist
checks.rationale: An account whose home directory is missing will get shell startup errors and, worse, some shells fall back to '/' as a working directory - the account still works, just in a confusing and potentially insecure state.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user account(s). All home directories exist.
checks.remediation: mkdir -p <home> && chown <user>:<user> <home>  # or fix the passwd entry if the path is wrong

checks.title: All interactive users' home directories are owned by that user
checks.rationale: If a home directory is owned by someone other than its account, that other owner can read/modify the account's dotfiles (e.g. plant a malicious .bashrc), functionally hijacking the account on next login.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 existing home director(ies). All correctly owned.
checks.remediation: chown <user>:<user> <home-dir>  # for each reported mismatch

checks.title: The shadow group has no members
checks.rationale: Members of the 'shadow' group can read /etc/shadow directly, which is equivalent to root-level access to every account's password hash - this group should stay empty on a hardened system.
checks.evidence: shadow group members: (none)
checks.remediation: gpasswd -d <user> shadow  # for each unexpected member

checks.title: Every group referenced in /etc/passwd exists in /etc/group
checks.rationale: A passwd entry pointing at a GID with no corresponding group is usually a leftover from a deleted group - if that GID gets reused later, the old account unexpectedly regains whatever access the new group carries.
checks.evidence: Checked 27 /etc/passwd entries against 59 known GIDs. All primary GIDs resolve to a real group.
checks.remediation: Create the missing group (groupadd -g <gid> <name>) or reassign the affected user(s) to a valid group with usermod -g.

checks.title: No legacy NIS '+' entries exist in /etc/passwd
checks.rationale: A line starting with '+' in /etc/passwd is a legacy NIS include directive; if NIS isn't in use (or is misconfigured), it can leave an unauthenticated wildcard entry that grants unintended access.
checks.evidence: Checked 27 line(s) in /etc/passwd. No '+' entries found.
checks.remediation: Remove any line starting with '+' from /etc/passwd.

checks.title: No legacy NIS '+' entries exist in /etc/shadow
checks.rationale: A line starting with '+' in /etc/shadow is a legacy NIS include directive; if NIS isn't in use (or is misconfigured), it can leave an unauthenticated wildcard entry that grants unintended access.
checks.evidence: /etc/shadow could not be read.
checks.remediation: Remove any line starting with '+' from /etc/shadow.

checks.title: No legacy NIS '+' entries exist in /etc/group
checks.rationale: A line starting with '+' in /etc/group is a legacy NIS include directive; if NIS isn't in use (or is misconfigured), it can leave an unauthenticated wildcard entry that grants unintended access.
checks.evidence: Checked 59 line(s) in /etc/group. No '+' entries found.
checks.remediation: Remove any line starting with '+' from /etc/group.

checks.title: The system default password hashing algorithm is SHA-512
checks.rationale: Weaker legacy hashing algorithms (DES, MD5) are fast to compute, which makes offline brute-force/dictionary attacks against a stolen /etc/shadow dramatically cheaper - SHA-512 (and PAM's rounds tuning) is deliberately slow to compute.
checks.evidence: /etc/login.defs ENCRYPT_METHOD YESCRYPT (expected SHA512)
checks.remediation: Set 'ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512' in /etc/login.defs, and ensure pam_unix.so in /etc/pam.d/common-password uses sha512.

checks.title: A default account inactivity lock period is configured
checks.rationale: Without a default INACTIVE period, an account whose password has expired stays enabled indefinitely instead of being automatically locked - useful for catching accounts nobody remembered to deprovision.
checks.evidence: /etc/default/useradd INACTIVE=None (expected INACTIVE set to a value >= 0)
checks.remediation: Set 'INACTIVE=30' in /etc/default/useradd (existing accounts also need: chage --inactive 30 <user>)

checks.title: /etc/motd permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: The message-of-the-day file should not be writable by non-root users, or a local user could plant misleading/malicious content shown to every other user who logs in.
checks.evidence: /etc/motd does not exist.
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/motd && chmod 644 /etc/motd

checks.title: /etc/issue permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: /etc/issue is shown before local console login; if writable by non-root it could be tampered with to display misleading prompts.
checks.evidence: /etc/issue: mode=644 owner=root group=root
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/issue && chmod 644 /etc/issue

checks.title: /etc/issue.net permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: /etc/issue.net is shown before remote (SSH) login when configured as the sshd Banner; if writable by non-root it could be tampered with.
checks.evidence: /etc/issue.net: mode=644 owner=root group=root
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/issue.net && chmod 644 /etc/issue.net

checks.title: /etc/issue does not reveal OS or version information
checks.rationale: A login banner that prints the OS name/kernel version/host info (via \m \r \s \v escapes) hands an attacker free reconnaissance before they've even authenticated.
checks.evidence: /etc/issue content: 'Ubuntu 26.04 LTS \\n \\l\n\n'
checks.remediation: Replace /etc/issue with a generic authorized-access-only warning, removing any \m \r \s \v escape sequences.

checks.title: /etc/issue.net does not reveal OS or version information
checks.rationale: Same rationale as /etc/issue: the remote-login banner shouldn't hand out OS/version reconnaissance before authentication.
checks.evidence: /etc/issue.net content: 'Ubuntu 26.04 LTS\n'
checks.remediation: Replace /etc/issue.net with a generic authorized-access-only warning, removing any \m \r \s \v escape sequences.

checks.title: /etc/motd does not reveal OS or version information
checks.rationale: Many distributions auto-populate /etc/motd (or update-motd.d scripts) with kernel/OS version banners at login; that's useful reconnaissance for an attacker who's already gained a shell and shouldn't be handed out unnecessarily either.
checks.evidence: /etc/motd does not exist.
checks.remediation: Remove OS/version-revealing content from /etc/motd and any /etc/update-motd.d/ scripts that generate it.

checks.title: GDM displays a login warning banner (if GDM is installed)
checks.rationale: On a system with a graphical login manager, the text-console banners in /etc/issue don't apply to GDM's own login screen - it needs its own banner-message setting to carry the same legal/monitoring notice.
checks.evidence: GDM is not installed on this host (checked for gdm3/gdm binaries and /etc/gdm3) - this is a headless/server system, so a GDM login banner does not apply.
checks.remediation: gsettings set org.gnome.login-screen banner-message-enable true && gsettings set org.gnome.login-screen banner-message-text 'Authorized uses only.'  (via a dconf profile/db for the gdm user, not interactively)

checks.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
checks.rationale: Scheduled jobs (log rotation, security scans, unattended-upgrades' own timer in some configurations) depend on cron actually running - an installed-but-stopped cron daemon silently breaks all of them.
checks.evidence: systemctl is-active cron: active; is-enabled: enabled
checks.remediation: systemctl --now enable cron

checks.title: /etc/crontab permissions are 600 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/crontab is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/crontab: mode=644 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 600, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/crontab && chmod 600 /etc/crontab

checks.title: /etc/cron.hourly permissions are 700 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/cron.hourly is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.hourly: mode=755 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 700, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/cron.hourly && chmod 700 /etc/cron.hourly

checks.title: /etc/cron.daily permissions are 700 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/cron.daily is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.daily: mode=755 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 700, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/cron.daily && chmod 700 /etc/cron.daily

checks.title: /etc/cron.weekly permissions are 700 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/cron.weekly is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.weekly: mode=755 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 700, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/cron.weekly && chmod 700 /etc/cron.weekly

checks.title: /etc/cron.monthly permissions are 700 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/cron.monthly is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.monthly: mode=755 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 700, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/cron.monthly && chmod 700 /etc/cron.monthly

checks.title: /etc/cron.d permissions are 700 or more restrictive, owned by root
checks.rationale: If /etc/cron.d is writable by non-root users, a local user could plant a job that runs with root's cron privileges, a direct privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /etc/cron.d: mode=755 owner=root group=root (expected mode <= 700, owner root)
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/cron.d && chmod 700 /etc/cron.d

checks.title: at is restricted to authorized users (at.allow present, at.deny absent)
checks.rationale: Same rationale as cron.allow (CIS-5.1.8 in checks/logging_audit.py): without an allow-list, any local user can schedule a one-off privileged-context job via 'at'.
checks.evidence: /etc/at.allow exists=False, /etc/at.deny exists=False (expected at.allow to exist and at.deny to not exist)
checks.remediation: touch /etc/at.allow && chmod 600 /etc/at.allow && rm -f /etc/at.deny   # list only trusted usernames, one per line, in at.allow

checks.title: Access to the su command is restricted to a defined group
checks.rationale: Without pam_wheel restricting su, any local user can attempt to su to root (still needing root's password, but it removes an easy detection point and lets any account brute-force-guess it).
checks.evidence: /etc/pam.d/su references pam_wheel.so: False
checks.remediation: Add 'auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid group=sudo' to /etc/pam.d/su

checks.title: pwquality minlen minlen >= 14
checks.rationale: A short minimum password length is the single biggest factor in how fast an offline attacker can brute-force a stolen hash.
checks.evidence: minlen is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'minlen = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality dcredit dcredit <= -1 (at least one digit required)
checks.rationale: Requiring at least one digit meaningfully increases the password keyspace against dictionary-based guessing.
checks.evidence: dcredit is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'dcredit = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality ucredit ucredit <= -1 (at least one uppercase letter required)
checks.rationale: Requiring at least one uppercase character increases keyspace against dictionary-based guessing.
checks.evidence: ucredit is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'ucredit = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality lcredit lcredit <= -1 (at least one lowercase letter required)
checks.rationale: Requiring at least one lowercase character prevents all-uppercase or all-numeric trivial passwords.
checks.evidence: lcredit is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'lcredit = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality ocredit ocredit <= -1 (at least one special character required)
checks.rationale: Requiring at least one special character further increases keyspace against dictionary-based guessing.
checks.evidence: ocredit is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'ocredit = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality maxrepeat 0 < maxrepeat <= 3
checks.rationale: Without a repeat-character limit, trivially weak passwords like 'aaaaaaaaaaaa' pass a pure length requirement.
checks.evidence: maxrepeat is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'maxrepeat = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality difok difok >= 2
checks.rationale: difok requires a new password to differ from the old one by enough characters that a trivial single-character rotation doesn't count as a real password change.
checks.evidence: difok is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'difok = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: pwquality retry 0 < retry <= 3
checks.rationale: Limiting retries during interactive password changes reduces the window for scripted guessing against the password-change prompt itself.
checks.evidence: retry is not set in /etc/security/pwquality.conf (not found) (pwquality default does not enforce this).
checks.remediation: Set 'retry = <value>' in /etc/security/pwquality.conf

checks.title: faillock deny is set to 5 or fewer failed attempts
checks.rationale: Without a bounded failed-attempt count, an attacker can brute-force passwords indefinitely with no lockout at all.
checks.evidence: /etc/security/faillock.conf deny = None
checks.remediation: Set 'deny = 5' in /etc/security/faillock.conf

checks.title: faillock unlock_time is configured
checks.rationale: unlock_time defines how long an account stays locked after hitting the deny threshold - without it set, the lockout duration falls back to a default that may not match this host's intended policy.
checks.evidence: /etc/security/faillock.conf unlock_time = None
checks.remediation: Set 'unlock_time = 900' in /etc/security/faillock.conf

checks.title: faillock even_deny_root is enabled
checks.rationale: Without even_deny_root, the lockout policy exempts the root account entirely, leaving it open to unlimited online password guessing.
checks.evidence: /etc/security/faillock.conf even_deny_root = None
checks.remediation: Add 'even_deny_root' to /etc/security/faillock.conf

checks.title: Password reuse (history) is restricted to at least the last 24 passwords
checks.rationale: Without a remembered-password history, a user can satisfy a forced password change by immediately rotating back to a password they've used before, defeating the point of periodic rotation.
checks.evidence: /etc/pam.d/common-password pam_pwhistory.so remember=None (expected remember >= 24)
checks.remediation: Add 'remember = 24' to the pam_pwhistory.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-password

checks.title: /etc/passwd permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root:root
checks.rationale: /etc/passwd is world-readable by design (it holds no secrets since shadow passwords split hashes into /etc/shadow), but must not be writable by non-root users or accounts could be tampered with.
checks.evidence: /etc/passwd: mode=644 owner=root group=root
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/passwd && chmod 644 /etc/passwd

checks.title: /etc/shadow permissions are 640 or more restrictive, owned by root:shadow
checks.rationale: /etc/shadow holds password hashes. If it is readable by non-root users, an attacker can take the hashes offline and crack them.
checks.evidence: /etc/shadow: mode=640 owner=root group=shadow
checks.remediation: chown root:shadow /etc/shadow && chmod 640 /etc/shadow

checks.title: /etc/group permissions are 644 or more restrictive, owned by root:root
checks.rationale: /etc/group defines group membership; if it's writable by non-root users, a user could add themselves to a privileged group.
checks.evidence: /etc/group: mode=644 owner=root group=root
checks.remediation: chown root:root /etc/group && chmod 644 /etc/group

checks.title: /etc/gshadow permissions are 640 or more restrictive, owned by root:shadow
checks.rationale: /etc/gshadow holds group password hashes and administrator lists; it must not be readable or writable by non-root users.
checks.evidence: /etc/gshadow: mode=640 owner=root group=shadow
checks.remediation: chown root:shadow /etc/gshadow && chmod 640 /etc/gshadow

checks.title: No world-writable files exist in key directories
checks.rationale: A world-writable file can be modified by any local user, which is a common path to privilege escalation or persistence if that file is ever executed or trusted by a privileged process.
checks.evidence: No world-writable regular files found under /tmp, /var/tmp, /home, /etc (20001 entries scanned (scan truncated at entry cap, more may exist)).
checks.remediation: For each reported file: chmod o-w <file>  (review the file's purpose first - some world-writable files, e.g. under a sticky-bit /tmp, are intentional).

checks.title: No unowned files or directories exist in key directories
checks.rationale: A file owned by a UID/GID with no corresponding account (e.g. left behind after a user was deleted) may be inadvertently accessible or reused by a future account created with a reused UID.
checks.evidence: No unowned files/directories found under /tmp, /var/tmp, /home, /etc (20001 entries scanned (scan truncated at entry cap, more may exist)).
checks.remediation: For each reported path: chown root:root <path>, or assign it to its correct owner after investigating why it's unowned.

checks.title: Local interactive user home directories are not group- or other-writable
checks.rationale: A group- or other-writable home directory lets other local users tamper with that account's dotfiles (e.g. plant a malicious .bashrc) to escalate privilege the next time the owner logs in.
checks.evidence: Checked 1 interactive user home director(ies); none are group/other writable.
checks.remediation: For each reported home directory: chmod g-w,o-w <home-dir>

checks.title: Default user umask is 027 or more restrictive
checks.rationale: A permissive default umask (e.g. 022) means every file a user creates is world-readable by default, including ones that shouldn't be.
checks.evidence: No UMASK setting found in /etc/login.defs (login.defs default of 022 applies).
checks.remediation: Set 'UMASK 027' in /etc/login.defs, and add 'umask 027' to /etc/profile.d/local-umask.sh for shell sessions.

checks.title: /tmp is a separate partition
checks.rationale: Isolating /tmp on its own partition lets it be mounted with nodev/nosuid/noexec and stops a full /tmp from taking down the rest of the filesystem.
checks.evidence: /tmp is a separate mount point (fstype=tmpfs, options=nodev,nosuid,nr_inodes=1048576,rw,size=16412504k).
checks.remediation: Add a dedicated /tmp entry to /etc/fstab (or a systemd tmp.mount unit) and remount.

checks.title: /tmp is mounted with nodev
checks.rationale: /tmp is world-writable by design; nodev stops it being used to plant device nodes as a privilege-escalation trick.
checks.evidence: /tmp options: nodev,nosuid,nr_inodes=1048576,rw,size=16412504k
checks.remediation: Add 'nodev' to /tmp's mount options in /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /tmp is mounted with nosuid
checks.rationale: nosuid on /tmp prevents a SUID/SGID binary planted there from having its privilege bits honored, closing a common local privilege-escalation path.
checks.evidence: /tmp options: nodev,nosuid,nr_inodes=1048576,rw,size=16412504k
checks.remediation: Add 'nosuid' to /tmp's mount options in /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /tmp is mounted with noexec
checks.rationale: noexec on /tmp stops binaries dropped there (e.g. by a compromised web app writing to a shared /tmp) from being executed directly out of it.
checks.evidence: /tmp options: nodev,nosuid,nr_inodes=1048576,rw,size=16412504k (expected 'noexec' among mount options)
checks.remediation: Add 'noexec' to /tmp's mount options in /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /var is a separate partition
checks.rationale: Isolating /var (logs, spool, package cache) stops runaway log growth from filling the root filesystem and taking down the whole host.
checks.evidence: /var is not listed as a separate mount point in /proc/mounts (it is part of its parent filesystem).
checks.remediation: Add a dedicated /var entry to /etc/fstab during install/repartition.

checks.title: /var/tmp is a separate partition
checks.rationale: Like /tmp, /var/tmp is world-writable and used for temporary files that can persist across reboots; isolating it enables the same nodev/nosuid/noexec hardening independently of the root filesystem.
checks.evidence: /var/tmp is not listed as a separate mount point in /proc/mounts (it is part of its parent filesystem).
checks.remediation: Add a dedicated /var/tmp entry to /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /var/tmp is mounted with nodev
checks.rationale: Same rationale as /tmp nodev: /var/tmp is world-writable and shouldn't be usable to plant device nodes.
checks.evidence: /var/tmp is not a separate mount point on this host, so the 'nodev' mount option does not apply.
checks.remediation: Add 'nodev' to /var/tmp's mount options in /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /var/tmp is mounted with nosuid
checks.rationale: Same rationale as /tmp nosuid, applied to /var/tmp.
checks.evidence: /var/tmp is not a separate mount point on this host, so the 'nosuid' mount option does not apply.
checks.remediation: Add 'nosuid' to /var/tmp's mount options in /etc/fstab and remount.

checks.title: /var/tmp is mounted with noexec
checks.rationale: Same rationale as /tmp noexec, applied to /var/tmp.
checks.evidence: /var/tmp is not a separate mount point on this host, so the 'noexec' mount option does not apply.
